samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers lead with a trimmed autoplay loop, split the motion into three labelled beats, and offer a 0.25x slow-motion version with the timings. B adds a timestamped filmstrip so people who won't press play can still follow the motion, and it explicitly says to write 'not yet tested' rather than imply results. A makes small unsupported claims, such as the beats overlapping to about 400ms in total, and its still-frame fallback is tucked into the Figma spec frame. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers put the clip first and split the motion into three labelled beats with 0.25x slow-motion versions. A does better on fallback: its timestamped filmstrip lets reviewers who skip the video still see the motion and check the timings, and it explicitly says to write "not yet tested" rather than imply results. B is strong on what to watch for and on asking pointed feedback questions, but it makes some unsupported claims: that the beats overlap to about 400ms total, that users "never wonder" whether the tap registered, and that Figma can't reproduce the arc. Its still fallback is also tucked inside the spec frame.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers put the recording first and break the motion into its three beats with slowed playback and a spec table. A is stronger on the fallback for people who won't play video: its keyframe filmstrip is meant to be read as a still, and it tells reviewers what to watch in its first line. A also refuses to invent results. B's labelled timecode overlay is excellent, but it guesses overlap timings it wasn't given, and it offers stills only as a stand-in for clips, not as a fallback for non-viewers. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers lead with the recording, split the motion into its three beats, use the 250ms and 400ms timings and suggest slowed playback. B does better on the fallback: it adds a keyframe filmstrip that reviewers can read without pressing play, and it tells them up front what to watch and in what order. B also says outright not to invent results, while A suggests a rationale sentence and adds a few general format tips that are less tied to presenting the motion.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers put the loop first, split the motion into three beats, and include the given timings along with slow-motion and filmstrip options. B is better on viewing order and what reviewers should look for: it gives an explicit post order, labelled slow-mo beats, a 'watch the 6s clip' cue, a filmstrip for people who won't play video, and pointed feedback questions. Both claim the motion takes 'under half a second', which doesn't fit 250ms + 400ms unless the beats overlap. A also adds some generic writing advice, such as credits and first person. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers put the loop first, split the motion into three labelled beats with a slow-motion view, and offer a filmstrip fallback. A is tighter: it uses an easy-to-check beat table and gives a clear post order with pointed review questions. B gives each beat its own loop, which is useful, but its sample caption says the total motion is under half a second, and that contradicts 250ms + 400ms unless the beats overlap. B also adds some generic writing and credits advice.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B explains more clearly what a hiring reader needs to see first (the work and decisions up front).
